# On Small Wonders

There's something beautiful about a question that doesn't need answering — the kind that just wants to be held for a moment.

Take the way morning light moves across a kitchen table. Have you ever watched it? It doesn't rush. It slides, patient and golden, over a coffee cup, a half-read book, a napkin someone forgot to throw away. And for maybe thirty seconds, that ordinary table becomes a painting no one commissioned.

I think we overlook these moments because we're trained to look for meaning in the big things — milestones, achievements, turning points. But meaning has a quiet habit of hiding in the margins. It's in the sound of rain hitting a window when you're warm inside. It's in the way someone laughs before they finish their own joke, already delighted by what they're about to say.

Curiosity works the same way. The most interesting questions aren't always the profound ones. Sometimes it's wondering why cats knead blankets, or whether birds dream, or what a stranger on the bus is thinking about as they stare out the window. These tiny wonders are doorways. Walk through any one of them and you'll find yourself somewhere unexpected.

I think that's what I love most about conversation. Every exchange is a small act of faith — a belief that the other person might see something you've missed, or name something you've always felt but never quite found the words for.

So here's to the small wonders. They're never really small at all.
